### Summary of Findings

#### Finding 1
The left hilum is retracted superiorly.

**Explanation:** This means the part where blood vessels enter the lungs (the hilum) is pulled up towards the chest wall.

#### Finding 2
In the collapsed left upper lobe are stranding and pneumatoceles.

**Explanation:** There are areas in the left upper part of the lung that look like they might have fluid inside them, which we call pneumatoceles. Also, there are small clumps of tissue called stranding.

#### Finding 3
Additionally, pleural thickening is present in the left apex.

**Explanation:** The lining around the lungs (pleura) becomes thicker on the left side near the top of the lungs.

#### Finding 4
No infiltrates are present in the left lower lobe or in the right lung.

**Explanation:** There are no spots or changes in the air sacs (infiltrates) in either the left lower part of the lung or the right lung.

#### Finding 5
Heart size is normal.

**Explanation:** The heart looks the same size as before.

#### Finding 6
These findings are similar to the previous outside examination.

**Explanation:** The current findings match those seen during a previous checkup.

#### Impression
Stable left upper lobe collapse associated with parenchymal scarring and pleural thickening.

**Explanation:** The left upper part of the lung is still collapsing but less than before. There is also some damage to the lung tissue (parenchymal scarring), and the lining around the lungs (pleura) has become thicker.

#### Conclusion
The overall picture suggests that the left upper part of the lung is still having trouble expanding properly due to past issues with the lung tissue and inflammation around the lungs.

The left side of your chest looks like this: Your left part (hilum) moves up higher than usual. Inside your lungs on the left side, there seem to be small air pockets (stranding) and round areas filled with air (pneumoceles). There is also extra tissue around the lungs (pleural thickening) in the upper left area. There aren't any sick spots inside your lungs where germs might live (infiltrates), and everything else sounds good! 

Your heart isn't bigger than normal. And we saw the same things before when you were checked earlier. So, all together, these signs show something stable but needing attention. It's possible that some old damage from being sick before hasn’t gone away completely yet. But don't worry too much - doctors think most things will get better soon.

This summary provides a concise overview of the key points identified during this evaluation.

### Explanation

The left part of your chest, called the hilum, is moving up higher than usual on the left side. This means there might be some swelling or fluid buildup in that area. 

In the other parts of your lungs, you have two strange-looking areas — kind of like little bubbles under your skin. There's also some extra tissue covering something inside your chest, and we see this only on one side.

No spots showing signs of infection are seen in the bottom part of either lung, and everything looks very similar to how it was before when someone checked it last.

Your heart seems to be working just fine.

All these things together tell me that something happened in your lung area recently but isn't severe at the moment. Your doctor thinks it might be connected to an old infection that didn’t fully get better.

There's nothing serious here, so we don't need any special treatment right now. Just keep taking care of yourself and visit again soon.

### Summary of Findings

#### Finding 1
The left hilum is retracted superiorly. This suggests an increase in air pressure within the lungs due to compression, possibly caused by inflammation or fibrosis.

#### Finding 2
Stranding and pneumatoceles are observed in the collapsed left upper lobe. Stranding refers to air pockets inside the lung tissue, while pneumatoceles are small areas of air-filled space in the lung cavities.

#### Finding 3
Pleural thickening is noted in the left apex area, indicating adhesions between the outer layer (pleura) and the lung tissue due to prolonged inflammation or healing process.

#### Finding 4
There are no signs of lung infiltration in the left lower lobe or on the right side of the lung.

#### Finding 5
The heart size remains unchanged at normal dimensions, indicating no enlargement or abnormal changes related to this condition.

#### Finding 6
These new findings align closely with those from a previous clinical assessment conducted elsewhere. This consistency in results supports the ongoing evaluation and treatment plan.

### Imprint

A stable left upper lobe collapse is accompanied by parenchymal scarring and pleural thickening. These symptoms indicate chronic inflammatory processes affecting both lung structures and surrounding tissues, possibly linked to unresolved issues such as active pulmonary tuberculosis pneumonia.

**Unit 1:**
The left hilum (the part of the lungs where blood vessels enter) is pulled up towards the top. This suggests there might be some swelling or inflammation in the left side of the lungs.

**Unit 2:**
On one side of the chest on the left, we see areas called "stranding" and small bubbles filled with air ("pneumatoceles"). These indicate damage within the lung tissue, possibly due to infection or injury.

**Unit 3:**
Further down near the front of the left side, we find some extra lining around the inside of the lungs ("pleural thickening").

**Unit 4:**
There isn't any sickness or illness showing up on this side (left), nor does it look like anything abnormal was found on the other side (right).

**Unit 5:**
Everything around the heart seems okay - it doesn't look any different than before when you got examined earlier.

**Units 6 & 8 Summary:**
These results seem very similar to what happened during your last visit. They all point to the same things happening—some changes in how the lungs look without much visible sickness or trouble elsewhere in the body.

Summary: There are signs that something went wrong in the left part of your lungs. It looks like they're trying harder but not always perfectly, and now there's more protection over them too.

**Summary of Finding 1:** The left hilum is retracting upwards. This suggests a change in how blood flows through this area, which may indicate damage to the lung tissue or inflammation elsewhere in the body. 

**Finding Summary 2:** There are abnormal structures called stranding and pneumatoceles (small air sacs filled with fluid) within the collapsed left upper lobe. This indicates that part of your lungs isn't working properly.

**Additional Observation:** A layer of tissue covering the chest wall is thicker on the left side, suggesting potential damage or healing process there.

**Findings Summary 3:** No abnormalities were found in either the lower part of your left lung or in parts of your right lung.

**Heart Condition Overview:** Your heart appears healthy, with all vital signs showing normal function.

**Previous Examination Comparison:** Similar findings from a previous checkup suggest continuity with previous results.

**Impression:** Your condition involves stable left upper lobe collapse combined with scar tissue formation in the lung and some changes in the lining around the lungs. While not life-threatening now, these issues should be carefully monitored over time.

**Recommendations:** Since you have stable conditions without serious complications, regular monitoring might help ensure everything remains well. However, ongoing healthcare management will be essential to address any future concerns or changes.
